## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

---

## 11. Navigation shell & sidebar

**One sidebar, every surface.** `AppSidebar` (`src/components/sidebar/app-sidebar.tsx`) is the single navigation surface for web, mobile, and the Chrome extension panel — there is no separate narrow IA. `ResponsiveAppShell` (`src/components/shell/responsive-app-shell.tsx`) renders it as a fixed left rail on wide viewports and, on narrow ones (≤640px, measured against the container with `useContainerQuery` — not `window.matchMedia`, which mis-reports inside the extension iframe), inside a Radix `Dialog` drawer behind a hamburger. Pass `embedded` so the sidebar fills the dialog content instead of positioning itself. Don't reintroduce a pill/section narrow shell.

**Drawers are Radix `Dialog`.** Any full-height navigation drawer goes through `@radix-ui/react-dialog` — it brings the focus trap, Escape, scroll-lock, focus-restore, `role="dialog"`, and unmount-when-closed (so off-canvas nav never sits in the tab order). Mirror `command-palette.tsx`'s narrow branch. Never hand-roll an off-canvas drawer with a `translate` + a plain scrim `<button>`. This is the nav drawer only; §8's Sheet ban still governs create/edit/configure surfaces, which stay routed pages.

**Sidebar vocabulary** (all in `app-sidebar.tsx`): `SectionHeader` (uppercase `text-sidebar-foreground/40` group label), `NavRow` (a router `<Link>` with the standard active treatment — `bg-sidebar-accent text-sidebar-accent-foreground` active, `text-sidebar-foreground/80 hover:bg-sidebar-accent/60` idle), and `AgentRow` (the agent name links to its chat; the chevron expands an inline accordion of config tabs, auto-expanded when you're on one of that agent's config tabs). Use the `sidebar-*` tokens; `sidebar-primary` (orange) is reserved for the single Build action. Status dots use `StatusDot` (`tone`: `amber` live / `destructive` failed / `muted` idle).

**Active state is path-derived, not stored** — compute it from `useLocation().pathname` (e.g. `pathname.startsWith('/$owner/<section>')`) so it survives reload and cross-org navigation.

**Active state is path-derived, not stored** — compute it from `useLocation().pathname` (e.g. `pathname.startsWith('/$owner/<section>')`) so it survives reload and cross-org navigation.

---

## 12. Page width & content column

The shell's `<main>` (`responsive-app-shell.tsx`) is full-bleed and sets **no** max-width — every page owns its own content column. To keep the column from jumping as the user navigates, there is one standard width.

- **`max-w-3xl` is the standard page content column.** Center it with `mx-auto w-full max-w-3xl`. This is what the shared agent shells (`AgentTabShell` / `AgentSubpageShell`, §13) and the top-level section pages (connectors, infrastructure, entity-types, inference-providers, environments) use. A new page defaults to this — don't invent a width.
- **`max-w-2xl` is the settings-form exception.** Account settings (`app/account/settings.tsx`) and organization settings (`organization-settings-page.tsx`) run a narrower column because a single-column settings form reads better tighter. This is the *only* sanctioned narrower width — use it for a settings-style form page, not for general content.
- **`max-w-6xl` is the wide-table opt-in.** The permissions matrix widens via `AgentTabShell`'s `className` prop (`max-w-6xl`) because it's a grid that needs the room. Reserve it for genuinely wide tabular content; pass it as an override, don't fork the shell.
- **Banned:** ad-hoc page widths (`max-w-xl`, `max-w-4xl`, `max-w-[…]`) on a page-level content container. If a page needs a width that isn't one of the three above, that's a signal to reconsider the layout, not to add a fourth width. (Narrow `max-w-*` on *inner* elements — a truncated label, a tooltip, an inline field — is fine; this rule governs the page column only.)

**Why one width:** when two sibling pages use different columns, content visibly reflows left/right as you move between them and the app feels unstitched. A single centered column across the section makes navigation feel like one surface.

---

## 13. Back navigation & sub-page shells

A detail, create, or nested page needs a way back to its parent. Reach for a **shared shell**, never a hand-rolled arrow — the app has two documented back-affordance families, and which one you use is determined by context, not preference. Don't introduce a third.

**Agent sub-pages → the `agent-subpage-shell.tsx` family.** Every tab and detail/create page under an agent (behaviors, skills, guardrails, permissions, identity, settings) wraps its body in one of these so no tab reads wider or differently-aligned than its neighbors:
- `AgentTabShell` — the plain centered `max-w-3xl` column for an index tab.
- `AgentSubpageShell` — a detail/create page. Pass `title` for a **centered sticky header** (`AgentSubpageHeader`: title centered under the tab bar, back arrow pinned in the left gutter so it doesn't pull the title off-center). Pass `showBack` for just the gutter arrow (`WithBackGutter`) with the page's own body below.
- `AgentCreatePageHeader` — a catalog/create route (New behavior, Add skill): **left-aligned** title with the back arrow beside it, matching the left-aligned agent header.
- The back control is an **icon-only** `ArrowLeft` (`size="icon"` ghost button, `h-4 w-4`, `text-muted-foreground hover:text-foreground`). No text label — the section name rides `aria-label` (`Back to <section>`) for screen readers; a visible "Back to Behaviors" just repeats the tab you came from.

**Section detail pages → the `DetailHeader` (`connectors/detail-header.tsx`) family.** The connector / connection / feed / deployment drill-down pages share one header so all levels look identical: a **`← Parent` back-link row**, then a left-aligned title row (`text-2xl` title · muted subtitle · status, baseline-aligned), then optional chips, then an optional error banner.
- The back affordance is a **labeled** link — `← Back to <Parent>` — using `DETAIL_BACK_LINK_CLASS` + `<DetailBackIcon>` (`ArrowLeft h-3 w-3`, `text-xs text-muted-foreground hover:text-foreground`). It reads as a breadcrumb because these pages are a drill-down hierarchy where naming the parent aids orientation.

**When each applies:** inside an agent's tab space → the agent shell (icon-only gutter arrow, title may be centered). A standalone section drill-down (connector → connection → feed) → `DetailHeader` (labeled `← Back to X` link, left-aligned title). The two differ deliberately — a centered title suits the agent tab bar's centered chrome; a labeled breadcrumb suits a multi-level drill-down. **Don't mix them** (no labeled link in an agent tab, no gutter-icon in a connection page) and **don't hand-roll a third** `ArrowLeft` at a new size or with a new label style. If you're building a page that fits neither family, extend the closer shell rather than starting fresh.

**Icon size is part of the contract:** `h-4 w-4` for the agent gutter arrow, `h-3 w-3` for the `DetailHeader` inline link. Matching the family means matching its size — a stray `h-5 w-5` or `h-3.5` back arrow reads as a different control.

---

## 14. Form action footers

**Use `<FormFooter>` (`src/components/ui/form-footer.tsx`) for a form's action row.** It renders `[Cancel] [Primary…]` right-aligned as a group (`flex items-center justify-end gap-2`), with Cancel as `variant="outline"` on the **left** of the primary action. Pass the primary button(s) as `children`; pass `onCancel` (and optionally `cancelLabel`, `cancelDisabled`) for the Cancel button.

- **Cancel is always `variant="outline"`, never `ghost`.** A ghost Cancel has no border and disappears next to the page; outline gives it a stable, consistent edge everywhere. (This holds for compact `size="sm"` inline footers too — smaller, still outline.)
- **Cancel sits left of the primary action, right-aligned as a group.** Never `[Primary] [Cancel]` (reversed), never Cancel toggled in the section header, never a full-width Cancel. `justify-end` on the row.
- **Don't hand-roll `<div className="flex justify-end gap-2">` with two buttons** when it's a form action row — that's what the primitive is for, and hand-rolled copies drift on variant and order (that's exactly how `ghost` Cancels and reversed pairs crept in). A raw `justify-end` row is fine for *non-form* button clusters (a toolbar, a card's inline actions); reserve `FormFooter` for the Cancel + submit pair.

**Destructive inline-confirms are a different pattern (§1), not a FormFooter.** The two-step confirm swaps the trigger for `[Confirm] [Cancel]` in place — there the destructive action leads and Cancel is the ghost escape hatch. Don't reach for `FormFooter` there, and don't apply the "Cancel is outline / Cancel leads" footer rules to a confirm swap.

+**Agent sub-pages → the `agent-subpage-shell.tsx` family.** Every tab and detail/create page under an agent (behaviors, skills, guardrails, permissions, identity, settings) wraps its body in one of these so no tab reads wider or differently-aligned than its neighbors:
+- `AgentTabShell` — the plain centered `max-w-3xl` column for an index tab.

+- `AgentSubpageShell` — a detail/create page. Pass `title` for a **centered sticky header** (`AgentSubpageHeader`: title centered under the tab bar, back arrow pinned in the left gutter so it doesn't pull the title off-center). Pass `showBack` for just the gutter arrow (`WithBackGutter`) with the page's own body below.
+- `AgentCreatePageHeader` — a catalog/create route (New behavior, Add skill): **left-aligned** title with the back arrow beside it, matching the left-aligned agent header.

+- The back control is an **icon-only** `ArrowLeft` (`size="icon"` ghost button, `h-4 w-4`, `text-muted-foreground hover:text-foreground`). No text label — the section name rides `aria-label` (`Back to <section>`) for screen readers; a visible "Back to Behaviors" just repeats the tab you came from.

+**Section detail pages → the `DetailHeader` (`connectors/detail-header.tsx`) family.** The connector / connection / feed / deployment drill-down pages share one header so all levels look identical: a **`← Parent` back-link row**, then a left-aligned title row (`text-2xl` title · muted subtitle · status, baseline-aligned), then optional chips, then an optional error banner.

+- The back affordance is a **labeled** link — `← Back to <Parent>` — using `DETAIL_BACK_LINK_CLASS` + `<DetailBackIcon>` (`ArrowLeft h-3 w-3`, `text-xs text-muted-foreground hover:text-foreground`). It reads as a breadcrumb because these pages are a drill-down hierarchy where naming the parent aids orientation.

+**When each applies:** inside an agent's tab space → the agent shell (icon-only gutter arrow, title may be centered). A standalone section drill-down (connector → connection → feed) → `DetailHeader` (labeled `← Back to X` link, left-aligned title). The two differ deliberately — a centered title suits the agent tab bar's centered chrome; a labeled breadcrumb suits a multi-level drill-down. **Don't mix them** (no labeled link in an agent tab, no gutter-icon in a connection page) and **don't hand-roll a third** `ArrowLeft` at a new size or with a new label style. If you're building a page that fits neither family, extend the closer shell rather than starting fresh.

+**Icon size is part of the contract:** `h-4 w-4` for the agent gutter arrow, `h-3 w-3` for the `DetailHeader` inline link. Matching the family means matching its size — a stray `h-5 w-5` or `h-3.5` back arrow reads as a different control.

+**Use `<FormFooter>` (`src/components/ui/form-footer.tsx`) for a form's action row.** It renders `[Cancel] [Primary…]` right-aligned as a group (`flex items-center justify-end gap-2`), with Cancel as `variant="outline"` on the **left** of the primary action. Pass the primary button(s) as `children`; pass `onCancel` (and optionally `cancelLabel`, `cancelDisabled`) for the Cancel button.

+- **Cancel is always `variant="outline"`, never `ghost`.** A ghost Cancel has no border and disappears next to the page; outline gives it a stable, consistent edge everywhere. (This holds for compact `size="sm"` inline footers too — smaller, still outline.)

+- **Cancel sits left of the primary action, right-aligned as a group.** Never `[Primary] [Cancel]` (reversed), never Cancel toggled in the section header, never a full-width Cancel. `justify-end` on the row.

+- **Don't hand-roll `<div className="flex justify-end gap-2">` with two buttons** when it's a form action row — that's what the primitive is for, and hand-rolled copies drift on variant and order (that's exactly how `ghost` Cancels and reversed pairs crept in). A raw `justify-end` row is fine for *non-form* button clusters (a toolbar, a card's inline actions); reserve `FormFooter` for the Cancel + submit pair.

+**Destructive inline-confirms are a different pattern (§1), not a FormFooter.** The two-step confirm swaps the trigger for `[Confirm] [Cancel]` in place — there the destructive action leads and Cancel is the ghost escape hatch. Don't reach for `FormFooter` there, and don't apply the "Cancel is outline / Cancel leads" footer rules to a confirm swap.

This clarifies the real convention. The connectors index uses `flex flex-1 flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6` — **full-bleed with `px-4`/`lg:px-6` gutters, no `max-w`**. Agents and events index pages have **no `max-w` at all** either. So the actual, consistent convention is:

My §12 draft got the *detail* side right but wrongly implied index pages should also be `max-w-3xl`. That's wrong — the picker card at line 301 confirms these index cards intentionally span full width. I need to correct §12 so it documents the **two-tier width system** accurately (full-bleed index vs. centered `max-w-3xl` detail), which is the real answer to your "width/centralization" concern: the jump between full-bleed and centered is *intended*, and the drift to watch for is pages picking the wrong tier or inventing a fourth width.

input.old_string:
The shell's `<main>` (`responsive-app-shell.tsx`) is full-bleed and sets **no** max-width — every page owns its own content column. To keep the column from jumping as the user navigates, there is one standard width.

- **`max-w-3xl` is the standard page content column.** Center it with `mx-auto w-full max-w-3xl`. This is what the shared agent shells (`AgentTabShell` / `AgentSubpageShell`, §13) and the top-level section pages (connectors, infrastructure, entity-types, inference-providers, environments) use. A new page defaults to this — don't invent a width.
- **`max-w-2xl` is the settings-form exception.** Account settings (`app/account/settings.tsx`) and organization settings (`organization-settings-page.tsx`) run a narrower column because a single-column settings form reads better tighter. This is the *only* sanctioned narrower width — use it for a settings-style form page, not for general content.
- **`max-w-6xl` is the wide-table opt-in.** The permissions matrix widens via `AgentTabShell`'s `className` prop (`max-w-6xl`) because it's a grid that needs the room. Reserve it for genuinely wide tabular content; pass it as an override, don't fork the shell.
- **Banned:** ad-hoc page widths (`max-w-xl`, `max-w-4xl`, `max-w-[…]`) on a page-level content container. If a page needs a width that isn't one of the three above, that's a signal to reconsider the layout, not to add a fourth width. (Narrow `max-w-*` on *inner* elements — a truncated label, a tooltip, an inline field — is fine; this rule governs the page column only.)

**Why one width:** when two sibling pages use different columns, content visibly reflows left/right as you move between them and the app feels unstitched. A single centered column across the section makes navigation feel like one surface.
input.new_string:
The shell's `<main>` (`responsive-app-shell.tsx`) is full-bleed and sets **no** max-width — every page owns its column. There are **two tiers**, chosen by page kind, not by preference. The jump between them is intentional; the drift to catch is a page picking the wrong tier or inventing a third width.

**Tier 1 — Index / list pages are full-bleed.** A section index (connectors, agents, events, infrastructure) renders a responsive card grid that should use the whole content area, so it takes **no `max-w`** — just consistent page gutters: `flex flex-1 flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6`. The grid inside is `grid grid-cols-1 gap-2 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3` (see §2). Exemplar: `app/$owner/connectors/index.tsx`. Don't wrap an index page in `max-w-3xl` — that strands the card grid in a narrow column with dead space on both sides.

  • evaluate                → run JS, get text back
  • navigate / scroll / wait_for_selector

Or Claude-in-Chrome text tools: get_page_text, read_page (CSS selector), javascript_tool, find.

# Browser-driven verification (authenticated)

For any UI verification that needs a signed-in session (past the auth wall), use the `agent-browser` CLI with a session cookie minted from the DB. The user's regular Chrome doesn't expose a remote-debug port, so `--auto-connect` will land on the wrong tab — mint a cookie instead.

## Scope

The forged session cookie authenticates the **web admin REST mounted at `/`** (`/api/auth/*`, `/api/<orgSlug>/...`, the SPA — anything `lobu apply` and the web app talk to). It does **NOT** authenticate the **public Agent API at `/lobu`** (`/lobu/api/v1/agents/*`, `/lobu/api/v1/agents/<id>/sessions`) — that path expects a JWT bearer from the OAuth device flow (`lobu login`) or a PAT. If `/lobu/api/v1/agents` returns `401` despite a valid cookie, switch to `lobu chat` / `lobu token`.

## Pick a target

Local dev backend (with prod DB attached over Tailscale): `https://<your-tailscale-host>.ts.net:8443`. Prod: `https://app.lobu.ai`.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)

# Session token from the DB (prod DB serves both targets)
DB="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
TOKEN=$(psql "$DB" -tAc "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Drive the browser

```bash
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify eval "document.cookie='__Secure-better-auth.session_token=$SIGNED; path=/; secure; samesite=lax'"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/<path>"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify wait --text "<expected text>" --timeout 25000
agent-browser --session lobu-verify snapshot -i      # find @refs
agent-browser --session lobu-verify click @e13        # interact
agent-browser --session lobu-verify screenshot --full /tmp/out.png
agent-browser --session lobu-verify close
```

## Driving the paired Owletto extension (connector debugging)

The cookie-forging above and `claude-in-chrome` both drive a *separate* browser that lacks the user's real logged-in sessions — Revolut, for instance, redirects them to `sso.revolut.com/signin`. To run JS or browser actions in the **paired Owletto extension** (the Chrome that holds the user's live sessions, which is what extension-scrape connectors like Revolut/LinkedIn use), go through the connector-operations bridge instead. No deploy required.

`lobu connector run` is the wrong tool here — it only does local Playwright/CDP against a `browser_session` auth profile, so it errors `Missing --auth-profile` for device-worker connectors (Revolut has no auth profile).

For one-off actions, the `lobu call` CLI is the quickest path (usually org `buremba`; connection id from `lobu call manage_connections --org buremba --arg action=list --raw`):

```bash
lobu call manage_operations --org buremba --arg action=execute \
  --arg connection_id=<chrome-connection-id> --arg operation_key=navigate \
  --arg input:='{"url":"https://app.slack.com/...","wait_for_load":true,"open_in_new_tab":true}' --raw
```

For multi-step scripts, use the SDK `operations` namespace via `lobu memory exec` / `run_sdk`:

```js
// chrome connection id: client.connections.list() → connector_key 'chrome'
const ops = await client.operations.listAvailable({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID });
// navigate opens a fresh background tab in the paired Chrome and returns tab_id
const nav = await client.operations.execute({
  connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID, operation_key: 'navigate',
  input: { url: 'https://app.revolut.com/transactions', open_in_new_tab: true, wait_for_load: true },
});
// evaluate runs arbitrary JS on that tab and returns the JSON-serialised result
await client.operations.execute({
  connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID, operation_key: 'evaluate',
  input: { tab_id: nav.output.tab_id, expression: '(async()=>{ /* read DOM */ return out })()', await_promise: true },
});
```

`operations.execute` → `dispatchChromeActionToExtension` (`worker-api/dispatch-chrome-action.ts`) → device-worker queue → the paired extension — the same bridge the office-bot Deliveroo connector uses. Chrome ops: `navigate`, `evaluate`, `get_accessibility_tree`, `wait_for_selector`, `click_ref`, `type_ref`, `screenshot`, `show_notification`, `network_intercept_*`, `close_tab`.

Gotchas:
- `search_sdk` does **not** surface the `operations` namespace (nor several others). Discover the real surface with `Object.keys(client)` inside a `run_sdk` script.
- Sessions that re-auth often (Revolut, ~hourly) must be freshly logged in *in the paired Chrome* right before you navigate+evaluate, or the fresh tab redirects to the sign-in wall.
- Per-call dispatch latency is 5–60s and virtualized lists recycle content out — for paginated scrapes, iterate inside the connector's own run, not via one-shot `evaluate`s.
- **Connector-side changes ship via re-apply, not the app release.** Per-org connectors (`examples/personal-agent`) live in `connector_definitions`/`connector_versions` and only update on `lobu apply` (or `connections.installConnector` for a single bundle). An app deploy that adds a *capability* (e.g. `show_notification`) does nothing until the connector that *calls* it is re-applied. **And a new chrome action also needs the matching handler in the extension build** — dispatching `show_notification` to an older installed extension fails with `Owletto for Chrome: unknown dispatch ... action_key='show_notification'`. So three things gate such a notification: an up-to-date extension build (the handler), a re-applied connector (the call), and macOS notification permission on the extension.

1. **Which target** the paired browser should open. The recipe drives `app.slack.com`/`app.revolut.com` etc. — but here you want it to open the **local dev app's pages**. The paired extension runs on your machine, so it can reach `http://localhost:8787` (the running backend) or `:5173` (Vite dev). The dev server is already up.

But there's an important reality check before I invest: the recipe notes the chrome bridge opens **background tabs** and per-call latency is 5–60s. "Open pages one by one to show how it works" implies you want to *watch* it happen in your visible browser. Let me find the chrome connection and confirm it's live first.

|---|---|

## 12. Page width & content column

The shell's `<main>` (`responsive-app-shell.tsx`) is full-bleed and sets **no** max-width — every page owns its column. There are **two tiers**, chosen by page kind, not by preference. The jump between them is intentional; the drift to catch is a page picking the wrong tier or inventing a third width.

**Tier 1 — Index / list pages are full-bleed.** A section index (connectors, agents, events, infrastructure) renders a responsive card grid that should use the whole content area, so it takes **no `max-w`** — just consistent page gutters: `flex flex-1 flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6`. The grid inside is `grid grid-cols-1 gap-2 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3` (see §2). Exemplar: `app/$owner/connectors/index.tsx`. Don't wrap an index page in `max-w-3xl` — that strands the card grid in a narrow column with dead space on both sides.

**Tier 2 — Detail / create / form / tab pages are a centered `max-w-3xl` column.** Anything that's a single flow of content or a form (a connector detail, a create route, every agent sub-tab, single-column management pages like devices / inference-providers / environments) uses the **full triad `mx-auto w-full max-w-3xl`** — all three classes, always together. This is what the shared agent shells (`AgentTabShell` / `AgentSubpageShell`, §13) and the section detail pages use. A new content/form page defaults to this.

- **`mx-auto w-full` is not optional.** A bare `max-w-3xl` (missing `mx-auto`) caps the width but **left-aligns** the column, so the page hugs the left edge while every other Tier-2 surface is centered — the content appears to shift sideways as you navigate. If you write `max-w-3xl`, write `mx-auto w-full max-w-3xl`. (This is the single most common width bug; devices / inference-providers / environments each shipped it before it was caught.)

Two sanctioned overrides on Tier 2, both narrow/widen the centered column — never a fourth freehand width:
- **`max-w-2xl` — narrow settings-form exception.** `app/account/settings.tsx` runs tighter because its single-column settings form reads better narrow. Use only for a settings-style form page. (Note: organization settings is *not* this — it's full-bleed like a section page; don't assume every settings screen is 2xl.)
- **`max-w-6xl` — wide-table opt-in.** The permissions matrix widens via `AgentTabShell`'s `className` prop because it's a grid that needs room. Reserve for genuinely wide tabular content; pass it as an override, don't fork the shell.

**Banned:** ad-hoc page-column widths (`max-w-xl`, `max-w-4xl`, `max-w-[…]`) on a page-level container. If a page needs a width that's none of the above, reconsider the layout rather than add a width. (Narrow `max-w-*` on *inner* elements — a truncated label, a tooltip, an inline field — is fine; this rule governs the page column only.)

**Why two tiers, strictly applied:** a full-bleed *form* looks lost (a 3-field form stretched across 1400px), and a `max-w-3xl` *card grid* wastes half the viewport. Getting the tier right per page kind is what makes width feel deliberate instead of random as you navigate. The failure mode is inconsistency *within* a tier — one index page full-bleed and its sibling boxed to `max-w-3xl` — which reads as the app coming unstitched.
